title: The Day-One Shortlist Checklist: Get on the Buyer's List Before They Call Sales
description: A 12-point checklist to get on a buyer's shortlist before they ever talk to sales, plus a weekly plan to stay in front of future buyers.
lead: This is the full day-one shortlist checklist from the reel. Most buyers pick their favorite vendors before they talk to anyone. This guide shows why that happens, the 12 things to check so you're on the list from day one, and a simple weekly plan to stay in front of future buyers.
insider: This is why we never run cold email as a one-time blast for clients. In one full quarter of steady sending we got a **3.69% reply rate**, because the same target market heard from us week after week. Showing up early is simple. Doing it every week, without a gap, is what we do for clients.

blocks.text: Why the shortlist is decided before you show up

In the [6sense 2025 Buyer Experience Report](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20251112018032/en) (more than 4,000 B2B buyers in North America, EMEA and APAC), **94% of buying groups ranked their preferred vendors before first contact** with any seller. They then **bought from that early favorite 77% of the time**.

6sense also found that [buyers put about **four of the five vendors** they evaluate on their shortlist from day one](https://6sense.com/science-of-b2b/buyers-are-even-less-of-a-blank-slate-than-we-thought/). So if you get added late, you are fighting for one open seat, against a favorite that already has a head start.
The lesson is simple. By the time a buyer fills in your contact form or answers your email, most of the decision is already made. You win by being known **before** they start looking.
What "day one" really means

Day one is the moment a buyer writes down the names they will look at. It usually happens in their head or in a quick team chat: "Who do we know that does this?" The names that come up are the ones they've seen often, recently, and in a useful way.

items: **Often:** they've seen you more than once. One email or one post is easy to forget.
**Recently:** they've seen you in the last few weeks, not last year.
**Useful:** what they saw taught them something or solved a small problem.

blocks.text: The 12-point day-one shortlist checklist
Go through each point and mark it yes or no. Every "no" is a reason a buyer might not think of you on day one.

head: Check
Yes / No
rows: You have a written list of the 200 to 500 companies most likely to buy in the next 12 months
You know the 2 to 3 job titles inside those companies who start the search
Every company on the list hears from you at least once a month (email, post or both)
You post something useful at least once a week, on the channel your buyers actually use
Your cold emails teach or offer something. They don't only ask for a meeting
Your website says in one line who you help and what result you get
Your website shows a price range or "from" price, so you're not cut for being a mystery
You have at least 2 case studies with real numbers from your buyers' world
You have a page comparing you to the usual alternatives (including doing nothing)
You're listed on the review or directory sites your buyers check
When someone types your category plus your niche into Google or an AI chat, you show up somewhere
You track which target companies reply, visit or engage, so you know who is warming up

blocks.label: Score it
blocks.text: 10 to 12 yes: you're in good shape. 6 to 9: pick the 2 easiest gaps and fix them this month. Under 6: start with points 1, 3 and 4. Without a list and a steady rhythm, the rest won't matter.
How to fix each part
Build the future-buyer list (points 1 and 2)

Your future buyers are companies that fit your best clients but aren't looking yet. Pull them from the same industry, size and region as your 3 best clients. Add the 2 or 3 job titles that usually start the search. This list is who you show up for, every week.
Show up on a rhythm (points 3, 4 and 5)

One email is a message. Twelve useful touches over a few months is a brand. Mix cold email with posts so the same name shows up in two places. Keep every touch useful: a short tip, a number, a checklist, a case study.
Make your website easy to shortlist (points 6 to 9)

When a buyer builds a list, they skim websites fast. If they can't tell who you help, what it costs or whether it worked for someone like them, they move on. Put those three answers on your homepage or one click away.
Be findable when they search (points 10 and 11)

Buyers check review sites, Google and AI chat tools before they call anyone. Search for your own category the way a buyer would. If you're not there, get listed, ask happy clients for reviews, and publish pages that answer the exact questions buyers ask.
The weekly plan

items: **Monday:** pick one useful idea for the week (a tip, a number, a mistake you see often).
**Tuesday:** post it on the channel your buyers use.
**Wednesday:** send a short cold email to the next batch of your future-buyer list, built on the same idea.
**Thursday:** reply to every response the same day. Note who is "not now" and when to come back.
**Friday:** check point 12. Which target companies engaged this week? Move them to a warmer list.

blocks.text: Worked example
Rough math to show why day one matters. Say **100 companies** in your market start buying this year. These are example numbers, using the 6sense rates above:

items: **94** of the 100 (94%) will rank their favorites before they talk to anyone.
If you are the early favorite in **10** of those deals, at a 77% win rate you'd expect about **7.7 wins** (10 × 0.77).
If you are a late add in **10** deals instead, the other 23% of wins gets shared by the other vendors. With about 4 others, that's roughly 5.75% each (23 ÷ 4), or about **0.6 wins** (10 × 0.0575).
Same 10 deals. About **7.7 wins** as the favorite vs about **0.6** as a late add.

blocks.text: The exact numbers will be different for you. The gap is the point: being early is worth more than being better on the sales call.
Common mistakes

head: Mistake
What happens
Fix
rows: Sending one big campaign, then stopping
Buyers forget you by the time they start looking
Send to your list every week or month, not once
Only emailing people who are "in market" now
You miss the 94% who rank vendors before contact
Build a list of future buyers and warm them up early
Every touch asks for a meeting
People learn to ignore your name
Make most touches useful on their own
No price on the website
Buyers cut you early because they can't judge you
Show a range or a "from" price
Case studies without numbers
Nothing sticks in the buyer's memory
Use real numbers from real clients
Posting where you hang out, not where buyers do
You're busy but invisible
Ask 3 clients where they read about your topic

blocks.text: Plan your weekly content with Claude

blocks.label: Day-one shortlist prompt
blocks.text:
I sell [what you sell] to [type of company, size, region].
The person who usually starts the search is: [job title].
My 3 best clients are: [short description of each].
The top problems my buyers have before they look for a vendor: [list 3-5].

Do three things:
1) Describe the companies I should put on my "future buyer" list: industry, size, signals that they may buy in the next 12 months.
2) Give me 8 weekly ideas. Each one is a useful tip, number or checklist this buyer would save, not a pitch.
3) For idea #1, write a short post (under 120 words) and a cold email (under 75 words) on the same idea. The email ends with a soft question, not a meeting request.
Use simple, plain English.

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.text: Show up before they search. Every week, not once.

faq.q: If buyers pick favorites before contact, is cold email useless?
faq.a: No. Cold email is one of the ways to become the favorite before they start looking. It works best when it's steady and useful, not one blast.

faq.q: How long does it take to get on day-one shortlists?
faq.a: It depends on your market and how long buyers take to decide. Plan on months, not weeks. That's why the rhythm matters more than any single email.

faq.q: What if I'm already a late add to a deal?
faq.a: Ask what they liked about the vendors already on the list and what's missing. Then show one clear way you're different. You can still win, but the odds are lower.

faq.q: Do I need to post on social media to do this?
faq.a: It helps, because buyers see your name in two places. If you can only do one thing, send steady, useful emails to your future-buyer list.
